title: How Do I Freeze My Credit at All Three Bureaus for Free?
meta_description: A credit freeze is free by federal law. Official freeze pages and phone numbers for Equifax, Experian and TransUnion, and how fast a freeze must be lifted.
answer: Freezing your credit is free by federal law, but you have to do it separately at Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion. The FTC says a freeze makes it harder for someone to open new accounts in your name, doesn't affect your credit score, and lasts until you lift it. When you apply for credit, you can lift it for free. The FTC says a bureau must lift a freeze within one hour if you ask online or by phone, or within three business days if you ask by mail.

steps.name: Have your details ready
steps.text: Each bureau will check that you are who you say you are. For mail requests, Experian asks for your full name, Social Security number, addresses for the past two years, date of birth, and copies of an ID and a bill or statement. Equifax says it may confirm who you are with questions from your credit report or a one-time code sent by text.

steps.name: Freeze at Equifax
steps.text: Go to equifax.com/personal/credit-report-services/credit-freeze and choose Place a Security Freeze, or call (888) 298-0045. Managing a freeze online takes a free myEquifax account, and you must be 18 to create one.

steps.name: Freeze at Experian
steps.text: Go to experian.com/help/credit-freeze, or call 1-888-EXPERIAN (1-888-397-3742). Experian says you no longer need a PIN; you manage the freeze with a free Experian account. By mail, write to Experian Security Freeze, P.O. Box 9554, Allen, TX 75013.

steps.name: Freeze at TransUnion
steps.text: Go to transunion.com/credit-freeze and create a free TransUnion Service Center account, or call 800-916-8800. TransUnion says a freeze added online or by phone typically takes effect almost immediately.

steps.name: Save your logins and confirmations
steps.text: Write down the email and password you used for each bureau's account and keep them somewhere safe. You'll need them to lift the freeze later. The CFPB says each bureau must send you written confirmation within five business days, including how to remove the freeze.

steps.name: Lift it when you apply for credit
steps.text: Ask the lender which bureau it will check, then lift the freeze only there, as the FTC suggests. You can lift it for a set time: TransUnion lets you schedule a lift up to 15 days ahead, and Experian lets you schedule a "thaw" with start and end dates. Put the freeze back when you're done.

steps.name: Keep checking your accounts
steps.text: The FTC says a freeze doesn't stop a thief from making charges on accounts you already have. Keep watching your bank, credit card, and insurance statements, and check your free credit reports.

details.heading: Freeze vs. fraud alert vs. credit lock
paragraphs: Credit freeze: Free by federal law since September 21, 2018, under the Economic Growth, Regulatory Relief, and Consumer Protection Act. You contact each bureau yourself. The FTC says a freeze lasts until you lift it and doesn't affect your credit score.

Fraud alert: Also free. The FTC says it tells businesses to check with you before opening new credit in your name, but unlike a freeze, it doesn't stop them from seeing your report. You contact one bureau, and it must tell the other two. An initial alert lasts one year and can be renewed. An extended alert, for people who've filed an FTC identity theft report or a police report, lasts seven years. An active duty alert lasts one year.

Credit lock: A product the bureaus sell, often as part of a paid plan. The FTC and CFPB say locks work in a similar way but may have monthly fees. The CFPB says locks are no more effective than freezes, which are free and which you have a right to by law.

details.heading: How fast a bureau must place or lift a freeze
paragraphs: Online or by phone: The FTC says the bureaus must place a freeze within one business day and lift it within one hour. By mail: they must place or lift it within three business days after they get your request.
Lifting is free, and you can lift a freeze for just a set period. TransUnion says a temporary lift can be immediate but suggests waiting a few minutes before the lender pulls your report.
If a bureau won't place or lift your freeze properly, the FTC says to call the bureau first. If that doesn't fix it, file a complaint with the CFPB at consumerfinance.gov/complaint or 855-411-2372.

details.heading: Why you may see different phone numbers
paragraphs: The FTC's IdentityTheft.gov lists general numbers for the bureaus: Equifax 800-685-1111, Experian 888-397-3742, and TransUnion 888-909-8872. The numbers on this page come from each bureau's own freeze page. TransUnion's freeze page lists 800-916-8800 for freezes, and 888-909-8872 for spouses adding or removing freezes for each other.

faqs.q: Does freezing my credit cost anything or hurt my credit score?
faqs.a: No. The FTC says there's no cost to place or lift a credit freeze, and it doesn't affect your credit score. You can still use your current credit cards and check your free credit reports while your credit is frozen.

faqs.q: How long does a credit freeze last?
faqs.a: Until you lift it. The FTC says a credit freeze lasts until you lift it, and Experian and TransUnion both say a freeze stays on your file until you ask to remove it. There's no need to renew it.

faqs.q: Is a credit lock better than a credit freeze?
faqs.a: Not according to the CFPB. It says credit locks are offered for a fee, often bundled with other paid services, and are no more effective than security freezes, which are free by law. A freeze is the option set out in federal law.

faqs.q: Can I freeze credit for my child or an aging parent?
faqs.a: Yes, with paperwork. The FTC says parents can get a free freeze for a child under 16, and guardians, conservators, and people with a valid power of attorney can get one for the person they represent. Each bureau has its own forms, often by mail. See the FTC's Credit Freezes and Fraud Alerts page at consumer.ftc.gov/articles/credit-freezes-and-fraud-alerts for links to each bureau's instructions.

faqs.q: Do I have to lift the freeze at all three bureaus to apply for credit?
faqs.a: Not always. The FTC suggests finding out which bureau the lender will use, lifting the freeze at that one bureau, and putting it back once the credit check is done.

warnings: Freezes are free at all three bureaus. If a page asks you to pay or start a subscription, you're looking at a different product, not the free freeze.
Type the bureau's web address yourself or call the number on its freeze page. Don't use freeze links or phone numbers from unexpected emails, texts, or calls.
No one needs you to move money to "protect" your credit. The FTC says it will never tell you to transfer your money to protect it.

target_questions: How do I freeze my credit at all three bureaus?
Is it free to freeze your credit?
How long does it take to unfreeze your credit?
What is the difference between a credit freeze and a credit lock?
What are the phone numbers to freeze credit with Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion?
uncertain: Phone numbers differ by source. The FTC's IdentityTheft.gov and 'Understanding Your Credit' list Equifax 800-685-1111 and TransUnion 888-909-8872. The bureaus' own freeze pages list Equifax (888) 298-0045 and TransUnion 800-916-8800, and TransUnion lists 888-909-8872 for spouse freezes. Experian is 1-888-397-3742 everywhere. The page uses the numbers from the bureaus' freeze pages and explains the difference.

The FTC's current 'Credit Freezes and Fraud Alerts' page (August 2025) doesn't give the one-hour and three-business-day timing. That comes from the FTC's 'Understanding Your Credit' page (November 2024), the FTC's September 21, 2018 press release, and the CFPB.

Two FTC pages disagree on whether a freeze affects applying for a job, renting an apartment, or buying insurance. 'Understanding Your Credit' says the freeze doesn't apply to those, so you don't need to lift it; 'Credit Freezes and Fraud Alerts' says you can temporarily lift it for them. The CFPB says the free-freeze rules don't apply to reports used for jobs, tenant screening, or insurance. The page doesn't take a side.

"Typically takes effect almost immediately" and the 15-day scheduling limit are TransUnion's own statements, not legal requirements. Experian's schedule-a-thaw feature is described on Experian's page. Equifax's page says you can temporarily lift a freeze but doesn't describe scheduling.
The 'Free credit freezes are here' alert carries a page date of June 23, 2022, but it describes rules that started September 21, 2018. Its source label leaves the date off.

Equifax's page says its value plans include a credit report lock and that 'our plans start at FREE.' It isn't clear whether a lock comes with the free plan, so the page relies on the FTC's and CFPB's description of locks.

The TransUnion page returned 403 to automated fetches, and the Equifax and Experian pages hide FAQ answers in collapsed sections. All three were read in a regular browser session on 2026-10-21. Experian's old freeze address (experian.com/freeze/center.html) now redirects to experian.com/help/credit-freeze/.
